overview.title: 📖 Overview: Building the Fire, and When the Sages Exaggerated
overview.subtitle: Tamid 29a–29b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The mishna continues describing the morning service: after clearing the ashes, priests built two wood arrangements on the altar — a large one for the daily offering, and a smaller one specifically to produce coals for the incense. Nearly any wood qualifies except olive and vine. This launches a broader Gemara discussion: Rava dismisses the mishna's claim of 300 kor of ashes and a golden drinking-cup for the lamb as exaggeration, prompting Rabbi Ami's famous principle that Torah, Prophets, and Sages all sometimes speak in hyperbole. Shmuel narrows this to exactly three rabbinic exaggerations — the ash heap, the Temple's golden vine, and its massive Curtain — while insisting the golden cup was entirely real, since 'there is no poverty in a place of wealth.' The daf closes with a dispute over exactly why olive and vine wood are excluded from the altar's fire.

callout.text: Any limbs or fats not fully consumed overnight were returned to the large arrangement to finish burning, before the priests descended to the Chamber of Hewn Stone for the next lottery.

slides.title: 📖 Rabbi Ami's Principle: Sacred Texts Sometimes Exaggerate
slides.subtitle: Prompted by Rava's skepticism about the ash heap and the golden cup

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rava: the mishna's claim of 300 kor of ashes on the altar, and giving the daily lamb water from an actual GOLD cup, are both exaggerations (גּוּזְמָא) — not literal facts
2️⃣ Rabbi Ami generalizes: the TORAH itself uses exaggeration — e.g., 'cities great and fortified up to heaven' (Deut. 9:1) — no one thinks cities literally reached the sky
3️⃣ The PROPHETS do too — 'the earth rent with the sound of them' at Solomon's coronation (I Kings 1:40) means the sound was very loud, not that the ground literally split
4️⃣ And the SAGES themselves speak this way — as in the ash heap and golden cup examples just discussed

callout.label: The lesson:
callout.text: Recognizing intentional hyperbole in sacred texts is itself a hermeneutical skill — not every vivid description is meant to be read with strict literalism.

slides.title: ⚖️ Shmuel's Three True Exaggerations
slides.subtitle: And why the golden cup does NOT belong on the list
rows: Ash heap (300 kor)
Yes
A vivid way of saying 'a great deal of ash,' not a literal measurement
The golden vine
Yes
Described as needing 300 priests to move — heavy, but not THAT heavy
The Curtain (paroches)
Yes
Also described as requiring 300 priests to immerse — genuinely massive, but the number is rhetorical
The golden cup for the daily lamb
NO — this was literal
Shmuel corrects Rava here: the Temple really did use an actual gold cup, since 'there is no poverty in a place of wealth' — the Temple spared no expense

slides.title: 🍇 Two of the Temple's Most Astonishing Treasures
slides.subtitle: The golden vine and the Curtain, in vivid (if slightly exaggerated) detail
slides.label: The details:
slides.text: A golden ornamental VINE stood at the Sanctuary's entrance, hung on posts; anyone could donate a gold leaf, grape, or cluster to add to it. Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok recounts that 300 priests were once needed to move it (an exaggeration for its true, still-impressive, weight). The CURTAIN separating the Sanctuary from the Holy of Holies was a handbreadth thick, woven from 72 strands of 24 threads each, in four colors (sky-blue, purple, scarlet, and linen) — 40 cubits long, 20 cubits wide, costing 820,000 gold dinars, with two new curtains made every single year. When it needed immersion, 300 priests were said to be required — again, an exaggeration, but a sign of its genuinely enormous size and weight.

slides.title: 🪓 Why Are Olive and Vine Wood Banned From the Altar?
slides.subtitle: Two reasons proposed, tested against consistency

lines.speaker: Rav Pappa
lines.text: Their wood has thick internal knots (קְטִרִי) — it burns poorly and produces excess smoke, unlike smooth, skewer-like branches that burn cleanly all the way through.

lines.speaker: Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov
lines.text: It's about conserving the Land of Israel — cutting down olive trees and grapevines, praised species of Eretz Yisrael, for firewood would be destructive to the Land's settlement and economy.

lines.speaker: Challenge to Rav Aḥa
lines.text: But if it's about conservation, shouldn't PALM trees (also praised species) be excluded too? Yet the mishna treats palm wood as fit!

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: The same challenge applies to FIG trees, which the mishna explicitly prefers — so both fig and palm wood in this context must refer to non-fruit-bearing varieties, which carry no such conservation concern.

summary.principle: The daily wood arrangement's construction reveals both practical craftsmanship (avoiding smoky, knotted wood) and a deeper concern for the Land's resources, while the Gemara's excursion into rabbinic hyperbole teaches that Torah, Prophets, and Sages alike sometimes speak in vivid exaggeration to convey scale — except when, as with the Temple's genuine golden cup, the reality was extravagant enough to need no exaggeration at all.

flowSteps.content: 🪵 Two wood arrangements built: large one for offerings, smaller one for incense coals — all wood fit except olive and vine
📖 Rava calls the ash heap and golden cup exaggerations; Rabbi Ami generalizes to Torah, Prophets, and Sages alike
⚖️ Shmuel narrows it to three real exaggerations — ash heap, vine, Curtain — while insisting the golden cup was literal

columns.content: 🍇 The golden vine and massive Curtain were genuinely enormous, if not literally requiring 300 priests
🪓 Olive and vine wood excluded — either for poor burning, or to conserve the Land's resources

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: recognizing intentional hyperbole in sacred texts is itself part of understanding them correctly

quiz.q: According to the mishna, which two types of wood were NOT fit for the altar's wood arrangement?
o: Fig and nut wood
Olive wood and vine (grape) wood
Pine and oak wood
Cedar and palm wood
quiz.e: The mishna states that all wood is fit for the arrangement except wood from the olive tree and the vine; fig, nut, and pine were the preferred choices.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Ami, which categories of sacred texts sometimes employ exaggerated (havai) language?
o: Only the Sages
The Torah, the Prophets, and the Sages all employ exaggerated language at times
Only the Torah
None of these sources ever exaggerate
quiz.e: Rabbi Ami states that exaggerated language appears in the Torah (e.g., 'cities fortified to heaven'), in the Prophets (e.g., 'the earth split' at Solomon's coronation), and in statements of the Sages.

quiz.q: According to Shmuel, which THREE things did the Sages describe using exaggeration?
o: The golden cup, the ash heap, and the Curtain
The ash heap, the golden vine, and the Curtain
The altar, the Menorah, and the Ark
The wood arrangement, the incense, and the daily offering
quiz.e: Shmuel specifies exactly three instances of rabbinic exaggeration: the massive ash heap, the golden vine (300 priests to move it), and the Curtain (300 priests to immerse it).

quiz.q: Why does Shmuel insist that the golden cup used to give the daily lamb water was NOT an exaggeration, contrary to Rava's view?
o: Because gold cups were common household items
Because 'there is no poverty in a place of wealth' — the Temple, as a place of abundant wealth, genuinely used an actual gold cup
Because the mishna about the golden cup is a later, unreliable addition
Because Rava later retracted his own opinion
quiz.e: Shmuel excludes the golden cup from his list of exaggerations, explaining that the Temple's genuine wealth meant an actual gold vessel was entirely plausible and real.

quiz.q: What challenge is raised against Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov's explanation that olive and vine wood are excluded to conserve the Land of Israel's resources?
o: That olive trees don't actually grow in Israel
That palm trees are also a praised species of the Land, yet palm wood is considered fit for the arrangement — requiring the answer that the mishna refers to non-fruit-bearing varieties
That the reasoning applies equally well to Rav Pappa's explanation
That the mishna never mentions palm trees at all
quiz.e: The Gemara challenges that if conservation were the reason, praised species like the palm (and even the preferred fig) should also be excluded — resolved by explaining that the wood used comes from non-fruit-bearing varieties of these trees.
